title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Developer sues Wixom over moratorium; what it means for power, water and local rules statewide.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight a developer is suing Wixom after the city extended its pause on new data centers, putting tax revenue and jobs on the line.
That sounds like it could set a precedent for all these moratoriums popping up.
Exactly. The lawsuit claims the moratorium exceeds local authority and blocks a planned project.
So what's the history here? How did we get to so many cities hitting pause?
It's been building for months. Proposals for large AI and server facilities have surged, and towns are worried about the scale.
What kind of scale are we talking about for power and water?
These facilities can draw enormous amounts of electricity for servers and cooling, plus significant water for those systems.
And that hits electric bills for everyone else on the grid, right?
Residents in places like Washtenaw and Oakland counties are already asking that question as deals move forward elsewhere.
Who are the main players in this Wixom case?
The developer on one side, city officials on the other, and Oakland County residents watching the tax revenue and job impacts.
What happens if the lawsuit succeeds?
The pause could be lifted, letting the project move ahead, but it might also pressure other cities to rethink their own rules.
We've seen Rochester Hills extend its moratorium another year just today.
Yes, and that keeps residents near potential sites protected from noise, traffic and power strain for now.
It also gives the city time to write permanent zoning standards.
Wixom is doing something similar, tightening rules before its six-month moratorium ends.
So the lawsuit could test whether these temporary pauses hold up legally.
That's the core question. Local authority versus developer rights under state law.
How does this affect farmland and small towns specifically?
Many proposed sites are on or near agricultural land, raising concerns about conversion and long-term community character.
And the tax revenue angle is big for local budgets.
Delayed revenue if projects are blocked, but also potential strain on services if they go through without proper planning.
What about the environmental side? Attorney General Nessel and green groups are appealing DTE deals for Saline data centers today.
Those contracts could affect electric rates and grid reliability for Washtenaw County residents.
The appeal focuses on protecting ratepayers from the massive new load.
Meanwhile Ypsilanti Township is vowing to fight a University of Michigan $1.2 billion project on the Huron River.
Over water use, traffic and local control concerns.
A U-M regent even called for a temporary halt yesterday over grid strain.
That shows the issue reaching inside the university itself.
Morley pushed back a hydro data center hearing to August 18 so residents can review power, water and tax details.
Small Mecosta County communities are really feeling the weight of these decisions.
State Sen. Gonzalez is touring the state to build support for tighter oversight.
Highlighting risks to electric reliability and water in rural and suburban areas.
East Lansing extended its freeze another year yesterday, blocking new proposals.
Residents in the broader Lansing region face similar risks if projects land nearby.
Kalamazoo commissioners are set to decide on a six-month ban soon.
That would give the city time to draft permanent rules before anything advances.
The pattern is clear: cities want breathing room to study impacts.
But developers see these pauses as overreach that stalls economic benefits.
The Wixom lawsuit will likely be watched closely by everyone involved.
What could the court decide and how fast?
It depends on the legal arguments around municipal authority, but a ruling could come in weeks or months.
Other towns drafting rules like Wixom will be taking notes.
Those standards on noise, power and water could become templates.
Residents 30 or 60 miles away might still feel ripple effects on regional power demand.
Exactly. The grid doesn't stop at city limits.
So what's the next step after the lawsuit filing?
Hearings, possible negotiations, and more cities weighing similar legal risks.
This could accelerate the push for statewide guidelines.
Or it could lead to more litigation if other pauses face challenges.
Either way, local control remains the flashpoint.
We should keep an eye on how these rules balance growth with protections.
The stakes for everyday ratepayers and neighbors are real.
Moving to quick hits now.
Rochester Hills voted today to extend its data center moratorium another year.
Residents near potential sites get more time before facing noise, traffic or power issues.
Nessel and green groups are appealing those DTE power deals for Saline data centers.
The outcome could shape electric rates and reliability in Washtenaw County.
Ypsilanti Township officials say they'll oppose the big U-M Huron River project.
Concerns center on water, traffic and keeping local say in the matter.
Morley delayed its hydro data center hearing until August 18.
That gives Mecosta County residents extra time to dig into the plans.
Wixom is already drafting new zoning and performance standards ahead of its moratorium end.
Those could influence how other Oakland County suburbs handle proposals.
Senator Gonzalez kicked off a tour today pushing for stronger state oversight.
Public stops across Michigan to discuss reliability and water risks.
Yesterday East Lansing extended its own data center freeze another year.
Blocking new applications while the city studies long-term effects.
A U-M regent urged a pause on the Ypsilanti Township project over grid concerns.
Highlighting potential rate impacts for nearby communities.
Kalamazoo commissioners will soon vote on a six-month moratorium.
That would halt proposals and buy time for permanent rules.
Now let's look at what's on deck for listeners who want to attend.
Tonight Speaker Township Planning Commission meets on an ordinance covering cryptocurrency mining, data centers including AI, and residential battery storage.
Tomorrow Negaunee has a public hearing on a proposed data center ordinance with limits to mining and industrial zones plus noise and height standards.
Also tomorrow the Michigan for Responsible Data Centers Coalition is holding a virtual town hall on Van Buren Township construction and regulations.
And on August 17 Kalamazoo City Commission votes on a resolution for a temporary moratorium on data center development.
Plenty of chances for residents to weigh in directly.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Wixom Lawsuit Tests Data Center Moratoriums Across Michigan
